column3: The Hebrew joins “the land and Jericho” with “and”; BSB makes Jericho the particular focus with “especially.” The last verb explicitly says they lay down.
The Hebrew explicitly says “from the sons of Israel”; BSB has “men of Israel.”
Close to the Hebrew.
After the two men, the Hebrew hiding verb has a singular object, “him”; BSB uses plural “them.”
The Hebrew says “for you will catch them”; BSB has “and you may catch them.”
The Hebrew uses “she” rather than naming Rahab, repeats “roof,” and describes the flax as laid out for her; BSB gives her the active role in laying it out.

The Hebrew says “the men” and uses pronouns for those pursued; BSB identifies them as “the king’s men” and “the spies.” The closing of the gate has an unnamed active plural subject, while BSB uses a passive.
The Hebrew has pronouns for both parties and explicitly says she went up “to them”; BSB names “the spies” and Rahab and adds “for the night.”
The Hebrew repeatedly links the clauses with “and that”; BSB introduces the last with “so that.”
“The Amorite” is a collective singular; BSB uses plural “Amorites.” The Hebrew sea name literally means “Sea of Reeds.”
The Hebrew has singular “our heart” and the image of spirit no longer rising in anyone; BSB has plural “hearts” and “everyone’s courage failed.”
The Hebrew specifies “the house of my father”; BSB uses “my family.”
The Hebrew explicitly says “our souls”; BSB has “us.”
The Hebrew says singular “our soul” and explicitly mentions dying; BSB has “Our lives for your lives.”
The Hebrew repeats that her house was in the wall and that she lived in the wall; BSB combines this into one explanation and explicitly names Rahab.
The Hebrew repeats “the pursuers”; BSB uses “they” at the second occurrence.
The Hebrew says “we are free of this oath”; BSB has “we will not be bound.”
The Hebrew positively instructs tying the cord and gathering the household, explicitly “the whole house of your father”; BSB makes both actions “unless” conditions and says “all your family.”
The Hebrew has plural “doors” and simply “outside”; BSB has singular “door” and supplies “the street.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says “they went” as an independent clause; BSB makes it “when they had gone.”
The Hebrew separately says they went, came to the hill country, and stayed there; BSB combines the movement and explicitly calls them “the spies.”
The Hebrew does not name the river after “crossed”; BSB supplies “the river.”
The Hebrew has singular “our hand”; BSB uses plural “our hands.”
